content: The medication efavirenz is commonly used in combination with other HIV medications to help control HIV infection. It works by reducing the amount of HIV in the body, which allows the immune system to function more effectively. This, in turn, lowers the risk of developing complications related to HIV, such as new infections or certain cancers, and improves overall quality of life. However, it is important to note that efavirenz is not a cure for HIV. To reduce the risk of transmitting HIV to others, it is essential to continue taking all prescribed HIV medications as directed by your doctor. Additionally, using effective barrier methods, such as latex or polyurethane condoms or dental dams, during sexual activity is recommended. Avoid sharing personal items like needles, syringes, toothbrushes, or razors that may come into contact with blood or bodily fluids. Before starting efavirenz, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it or have any other allergies. This medication may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other issues. Efavirenz can also affect the heart's rhythm, potentially causing a condition known as QT prolongation. The risk of QT prolongation may be higher if you have certain medical conditions, such as low potassium or magnesium levels, or if you are taking other medications that can cause QT prolongation. Severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting can also increase this risk. Inform your doctor if you are taking diuretics (water pills) or experiencing any of these conditions. Efavirenz may cause dizziness, drowsiness, or difficulty concentrating. Alcohol or marijuana (cannabis) can worsen these effects. It is also advisable to avoid alcoholic beverages while taking this medication. In children, rashes are more common and may be more serious. If a rash develops, report it to your doctor immediately. In some cases, an antihistamine may be prescribed for children before starting efavirenz to reduce the risk of rash. During pregnancy, this medication should only be used when clearly needed, as it may pose risks. However, efavirenz may be part of a treatment plan to reduce the risk of transmitting HIV to your baby. This medication can pass into breast milk, so discuss breastfeeding with your doctor. Efavirenz can interact with other medications, potentially altering how they work or increasing the risk of side effects. It may also speed up the removal of certain drugs from the body, reducing their effectiveness. Inform your doctor and pharmacist about all the products you use, including prescription and non-prescription drugs, as well as herbal supplements. Some HIV medications, such as elvitegravir, etravirine, nevirapine, or rilpivirine, may interact with efavirenz. If you are taking atazanavir, you may also need to take ritonavir. Additionally, efavirenz may reduce the effectiveness of hormonal birth control methods, such as pills, patches, or rings, which could result in pregnancy. Discuss reliable backup birth control methods with your doctor or pharmacist. When taking efavirenz, follow your doctor's instructions carefully. Take the medication on an empty stomach, usually once daily at bedtime, as taking it with food can increase the risk of side effects. Swallow the medication whole with water. If you have difficulty swallowing the capsule, it can be opened, and the contents mixed with a small amount of soft food, such as applesauce, grape jelly, or yogurt. Consume the mixture within 30 minutes and avoid eating for two hours afterward. For infants who cannot eat solid foods, the contents can be mixed with infant formula and administered using an oral syringe. Common side effects of efavirenz include dizziness, trouble sleeping, drowsiness, unusual dreams, and difficulty concentrating. These effects often begin within 1-2 days of starting the medication and typically resolve within 2-4 weeks. Taking efavirenz on an empty stomach at bedtime can help reduce these side effects. Avoid alcohol and recreational drugs while taking this medication. Notify your doctor if you experience any severe or persistent side effects. As your immune system strengthens, it may begin to fight off infections you already had, potentially causing symptoms to reappear. In some cases, an overactive immune response may occur, which can happen shortly after starting HIV treatment or even months later. Changes in body fat distribution, such as increased fat in the upper back and stomach or decreased fat in the arms and legs, may also occur. The cause and long-term effects of these changes are not yet fully understood. If you miss a dose of efavirenz, take it as soon as you remember. If it is close to the time of your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not double the dose to catch up. Store the medication at room temperature, away from light and moisture, and do not store it in the bathroom. Properly discard expired or unused medication as instructed by your pharmacist. If you suspect an overdose or experience severe symptoms such as passing out or difficulty breathing, call emergency services (911) or a poison control center immediately. In the U.S., you can contact the poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about efavirenz. It is not a substitute for professional medical advice. Always consult your healthcare provider for complete information about this medication and your specific health needs.
